extracted.intended_audience: general public and health-interested readers (including clinicians, journalists, and policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate clinical, regulatory, and research-quality evidence about ivermectin's use for COVID-19, and identify misinformation, ethical, and policy considerations. Useful for readers assessing claims, guidelines, or research on ivermectin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory/clinical guidance against routine use
rubrics_metrics.description: The WHO, the European Medicines Agency (EMA), the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) all do not advise using ivermectin in an attempt to treat or prevent COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple national and international bodies advise against use of ivermectin for prevention or treatment of COVID‑19 outside well-designed clinical trials; policies include non-authorization within the EU and the FDA's statement that ivermectin is not approved for any viral illness. NIH states insufficient evidence to recommend for or against its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use only within well-designed clinical trials for COVID-19
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory bodies (EMA, WHO) explicitly advise that available data do not support use for COVID-19 'outside well-designed clinical trials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where uncertainty exists, rely on randomized, adequately powered, controlled clinical trials to determine efficacy and safety rather than anecdote, preprints, or small/poor-quality studies. Large trials (e.g., ACTIV-6) are cited as necessary and have found no effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological plausibility and dose-exposure criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In vitro studies showed antiviral effects with an IC50 of ~2.2–2.8 μM, but doses much higher than maximum approved or safely achievable for humans would be required for an antiviral effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims against whether effective concentrations observed in vitro are achievable and safe in humans; beware of extrapolating cell-culture antiviral activity to clinical efficacy without pharmacokinetic plausibility. High doses may be toxic and are not covered by human-use approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toxicity and therapeutic window concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The antiviral mechanism is believed to involve suppression of a host cellular process (inhibition of nuclear transport by importin α/β1), and drugs inhibiting that process at therapeutic doses have failed due to systemic toxicity and narrow therapeutic windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the safety profile and therapeutic window before considering off-label antiviral use; absence of demonstrated safe, effective dosing for COVID-19 undermines off-label adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological quality and evidence certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Many studies on ivermectin for COVID‑19 have serious methodological limitations, resulting in very low evidence certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating studies, check for common methodological problems (small sample size, lack of randomization, inadequate blinding, early stopping, selective reporting) and downgrade confidence where such limitations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data integrity, transparency, and retraction risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Several publications supporting ivermectin efficacy were retracted due to errors, unverifiable data, ethical concerns, or suspected falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require raw data availability, independent verification, and ethical approvals; treat findings from studies later retracted or with unverifiable data with extreme caution; retractions can substantially distort meta-analyses and public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-analysis methodology standards (anti-pattern checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading meta-analyses during the pandemic violated norms: inclusion of studies with widely different dosages, open-label designs, poor-quality control groups (or none), unpublished ad-hoc trials, and incompatible outcome measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good meta-analyses should (a) pre-specify inclusion criteria, (b) assess and account for heterogeneity in doses/designs/outcomes, (c) prefer peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials, and (d) avoid combining fundamentally incompatible or low-quality studies. Failure to do so can produce spurious positive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review and publication status weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Many misleading claims were based on preprints or unpublished trials that had not undergone peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat preprints and non-peer-reviewed reports as preliminary; weight peer-reviewed, reproducible RCT evidence more heavily when making clinical or policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and informed consent for population interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mexico City distribution of ivermectin was withdrawn by SocArXiv citing concerns it was effectively an experiment carried out on people without gaining informed consent; ethics concerns led to withdrawals and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass distribution or programmatic use of unproven treatments requires ethical review and informed consent; absence of consent or ethics approval undermines the legitimacy of reported outcomes and can cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific clinical exception: treat strongyloidiasis risk before corticosteroids
rubrics_metrics.description: People infected with Strongyloides stercoralis are at risk for hyperinfection syndrome if given corticosteroids; WHO, ECDC, PHAC and CDC recommend presumptive treatment for strongyloidiasis with ivermectin in people at high or moderate risk before or with corticosteroids when managing COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ivermectin's role as appropriate treatment for a parasitic infection in a defined clinical context (prevention of SHS) and use as an antiviral for COVID‑19; lists of high- and moderate-risk regions are provided and treatment in this context is for the parasite, not for COVID-19 itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid human use of veterinary formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people took veterinary preparations of ivermectin, which led to poisonings and shortages; the CDC issued a health alert about increased poison-control calls, and the FDA warned against such use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use veterinary products for self-treatment; veterinary formulations are not dosed/regulated for human use and can cause severe harm. Public messaging should discourage this practice and regulators should monitor related harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory status and off-label use transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ivermectin is not approved by the FDA to treat viral illnesses and is not authorized for COVID‑19 in the EU; some countries nevertheless allowed off-label or compassionate use, with some later rescinded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers and clinicians should be transparent about regulatory status, basis for off-label decisions, and the evidence justifying any compassionate-use program; programs should be revocable if evidence or ethics concerns emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of misinformation and deceptive sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading meta-analysis websites had anonymous owners, multiple domains redirecting to the same content, colourful but misleading graphics, and used servers previously used to spread other misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess provenance, authorship transparency, domain patterns, server reuse, and methodological transparency to detect potentially deceptive sources. Anonymous or networked sites making strong claims without methodological detail are high-risk misinformation sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake endorsements and source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: False tweets and fabricated quotations (e.g., purported endorsements by William C. Campbell) circulated claiming expert support for ivermectin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify endorsements by checking primary sources and direct statements from named individuals or institutions; be skeptical of viral images/quotes without traceable, original citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and commercial incentives disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases cited where researchers or companies filed patents, profited from increased demand, or failed to disclose conflicts of interest (e.g., patent filings for drug combinations; companies benefiting from ivermectin sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require COI disclosure for researchers and commentators; scrutinize financial incentives or patent activity that may bias study design, interpretation, or promotion of treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and social drivers that affect prescribing and uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribing trends correlated with political affiliation (e.g., Republican-voting areas showed surges in ivermectin prescriptions); ivermectin became politicized and championed by particular political and social groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims or utilization trends, account for non-clinical drivers (political advocacy, social-media influencers, organized networks) that can distort medical decision-making and public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal accountability and consent in institutional settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal actions have arisen where ivermectin was given without consent (Arkansas inmates lawsuit) and disputes over public health messaging (FDA social media posts resulted in litigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure informed consent and institutional oversight for treatments in custodial or institutional settings; regulators and agencies should be cautious in public messaging to avoid overstepping statutory authority while still communicating risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/IP context as relevant to interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: With ivermectin patent expired, generic manufacturers profited from demand spikes; claims that no one would profit were contradicted by patent filings and revenue increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider economic drivers and IP status when assessing promotion/uptake of treatments; skepticism is warranted where claims about lack of profit motives conflict with observable commercial activity.
